citations.review_text: A truly atrocious interface... so many pop ups... going away from the standard civ interface will be the death of the franchise.

Dev response: It looks like a mobile UI. On top of everything, the game had obnoxious notifications/help boxes. I couldn't even continue. That is how bad it was.

I imagine I would hate the age stuff too, though never got that far. And I suppose its very likely that you have not improved the AI either since forever. And I refunded on a 50% sale. It wasnt even worth that. Not even sure I would bother if the game was free. That is how bad it is.

**Not Recommended**

I have been playing Civilization since the beginning, and after my first hour with Civilization VII, I am stunned by how deeply flawed and unfinished it feels.

This is about as close as a game can come to breaking a beloved brand.

The interface is horrific. Basic information is difficult to find, menus are awkward and unintuitive, and the whole experience constantly gets between the player and the game. There are odd glitches and rough edges everywhere. Instead of feeling like a polished entry in one of the most important strategy franchises ever made, it often feels cheap and held together with spit and a prayer.

At times, it is practically unplayable. Not because the underlying strategy is necessarily bad, but because interacting with it is so unpleasant.

The frustrating part is that I can see worthwhile ideas underneath the mess. Some of the gameplay changes are interesting, and I think several of them could ultimately help the franchise evolve. I am not opposed to Civilization changing. The series should experiment, and it should try to solve problems such as late-game stagnation, excessive micromanagement and predictable campaign pacing.

But good ideas do not excuse this level of execution.

The music is excellent, and the soundscape is rich, lush and worthy of Civilization. Unfortunately, the presentation surrounding the actual gameplay feels unfinished, confusing and shockingly below the standard this franchise has earned.

I want Civilization VII to survive this. The hardcore fans may be the only reason it gets enough time and support to become the game it should have been. But that will require more than patches around the edges. The interface and overall user experience need fundamental reconstruction.

Firaxis: this needs to get dramatically better. In its current state, it is not acceptable.

I've been a fan of Civilization since the very first game, but this one feels more like Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth than a traditional Civilization title.

After millions of clicks, it feels like every turn is filled with silly choices, random bonus packs, "deals," and surprise events. I've never felt so tired of constantly clicking through pop-ups and notifications instead of focusing on strategy.

The game also feels very unbalanced. Expansion is far too easy—I can produce a Settler every few turns and simply spam cities across the entire planet with little challenge or consequence.

Overall, I found the gameplay repetitive, unbalanced, and, unfortunately, quite boring compared to previous Civilization games.  I've only played for about an hour, and I already feel like uninstalling it.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the user interface and user experience as muddy, difficult to read, and lacking clear visibility of districts, yields, and resources from a bird's-eye view.

citations.review_text:
It breaks my heart that I cannot still recommend this game. The newest Test of Time update really improved the game a LOT. It feels clearer, I enjoy the options, and the map generation is way better than on launch. So, for that, I give congratulations for trying to make the game better with so many big overhauls.

But sadly, the foundation is still poor, so it will take more to bring it to a recommended state. If they add the final information/future age, like in previous Civ, and update the UI/UX just a little bit more, I think that might push it into the recommended range for me personally. I really miss the information era stuff from CIV 6, but that may be just me.

A big issue for me is also just visual clarity. Once I get into the modern age, it's so hard to know what anything even is. The cities are beautiful up close, but all mesh together into one from a normal view. This is something that CIV 6 does masterfully with its color variety; everything in CIV 7 feels like a gray blob of buildings.

Either way, I am a big fan of this series, and I wish you the best in improving this game. I am more than willing to change my review to recommended if it keeps improving.

It just isn't very engaging.

In an attempt to solve perceived issues from the previous game, Firaxis heavily stripped down the gameplay and left us with a husk of what the series used to be. Even with the Test of Time Update, there isn't much going on; and this is during the Early game which has historically been the most exciting time during a campaign.

Some head-scratching decisions make the game worse as well. The new Town mechanic slows expansion down to a crawl, city limits actively punish you for building beyond your cap, and Towns count towards the cap. This isn't even like other modern 4X games, where Outposts can be built freely without impacting the cap.

The UI is also significantly worse. From a pure readability perspective, it is muddy and everything is difficult to find. Unlike previous games, where you could take a bird's eye view and instantly know the location of every district/yield/resource.

As a positive, combat is significantly improved. Commanders are a much better way to deal with the age-old problem of unit bloat, and AI is actually intelligent enough to use them properly.

Ultimately, the new Test of Time update isn't enough to make this worth buying at full price. Even on sale, this one struggles as a worthwhile successor to the legendary Civilization franchise.

Treat Civ VII like a reboot, not a continuation of what we love about the series.

For the developers

I would recommend checking out some of the UI mods available on Steam workshop. There are plenty of examples of items that significantly improve readability and usability.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the user interface suffers from readability issues and is difficult to comprehend, with muddy visuals where buildings visually merge together from a standard perspective.

citations.review_text:
As someone who has spent countless hours with every entry in the series since the Amiga 500 era of Civilization I, I’m writing this as a long time fan of the franchise.

I know firsthand that these games can become a genuinely good companion during difficult times. Still, I’ll try to be as objective as possible.

Under normal circumstances, I would have pre ordered the game immediately. However, after seeing both the gameplay mechanics and the art direction, I decided not to buy it for quite a while. Unfortunately, despite the strong backlash against Civilization VI’s visual style, which felt designed around a more mobile oriented aesthetic that likely appealed to younger audiences, a similar issue still exists here. The UI design, frankly, is difficult to comprehend.

Before getting into the pros and cons, though, it’s worth mentioning something important: since Civilization V, these games have generally taken around two years of patches before reaching a truly polished and mature state. I’m not defending that practice, in fact, I dislike it, but that has become the reality of the series. So there is still time for the current Civilization to improve significantly.

Pros:

Probably the best combat system the series has ever had. The general system for land, naval, and air warfare and its perks are intelligently designed. The framework has real potential, and I hope they continue expanding it with future updates.

The city state system can arguably be considered better than the one in Civ VI.

The new district system is controversial, but overall I’d say it leans slightly more toward good than bad.

Strangely enough, and sadly, in its current state, there aren’t many newly added or improved mechanics that make me say, “this was genuinely well designed.”

Cons:

Yes, we can continue with the same civilization across eras, but the age transition system is honestly baffling. When an age ends, wars automatically end as well. So you get situations where three civilizatio…

It breaks my heart that I cannot still recommend this game. The newest Test of Time update really improved the game a LOT. It feels clearer, I enjoy the options, and the map generation is way better than on launch. So, for that, I give congratulations for trying to make the game better with so many big overhauls.

But sadly, the foundation is still poor, so it will take more to bring it to a recommended state. If they add the final information/future age, like in previous Civ, and update the UI/UX just a little bit more, I think that might push it into the recommended range for me personally. I really miss the information era stuff from CIV 6, but that may be just me.

A big issue for me is also just visual clarity. Once I get into the modern age, it's so hard to know what anything even is. The cities are beautiful up close, but all mesh together into one from a normal view. This is something that CIV 6 does masterfully with its color variety; everything in CIV 7 feels like a gray blob of buildings.

Either way, I am a big fan of this series, and I wish you the best in improving this game. I am more than willing to change my review to recommended if it keeps improving.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that age transitions trigger resets that clear out trade routes and resource assignments while ending wars and diplomatic relationships.

citations.review_text:
After spending some time with the game, I've come to the conclusion that Civilization VII doesn't want me to build a civilization. It wants me to manage systems with menus and the "Magic Button™"

Magic Button™ is what I refer to when instead of systems that used to be visualized (things like builder units) have now been condensed into menus with one-click outcomes. No showing of processes, only telling outcomes.

Civilization used to be about building an empire, watching it grow over hundreds of years, and becoming attached to the story that emerged. Civ VII seems more interested in making sure every mechanic has a menu, every menu has a currency, every currency has a synergy, and every synergy grants +1 shoelace coupon to naval units situated in a river next to a mango plantation during a full moon.


The age transition system might be the single most baffling design decision in Civilization history. 

Imagine spending hours building your civilization only for the game to periodically walk into the room, sweep everything off your desk, and proudly announce “Oh, you had plans for that thing you were doing? Look at me! I'm the captain now.”

Trade routes? Reset.

Resource assignments? Reset.

Wars? Everybody suddenly got over it.

Units? Need new orders.

Missionaries? Lost their faith I guess.

Advisors? “Would you like some advice now? How about now? … Now?”

No, thanks. I choose life.

The entire system feels less like history progressing and more like somebody repeatedly loading an autosave from an alternate timeline. The loss of continuity affects almost everything.

Independent villages can completely change into something else between ages. Others disappear entirely. Relationships you've built no longer matter. Civilization is supposed to be about watching societies develop through time. Instead, Civ VII occasionally shrugs and says, "Nah, that boring. What if this?"

Military units suffer from the same problem. In previous games, units earned promotions and …

claims.claim: Reviewers report that important mechanics and fundamental systems are poorly explained, leaving players to discover them dozens of hours into the game.

citations.review_text: Civ VII has some strong ideas. I like the three-Age structure, civilization transitions, settlement specialization, and the deeper economic systems. But many important mechanics are poorly explained, and I'm still discovering fundamental systems dozens of hours in. The one-more-turn pull isn't as strong for me as Civ V or VI yet. I'm enjoying learning it and expect to keep playing, but I wouldn't recommend paying full price until you know the new Age and civilization systems appeal to you.

Context: while many of the original negative reviews for Civ VII were from long-time users frustrated by the new game dynamics, I am new to the series. i decided to purchase when the major fix / update was released in early summer 2026, which addressed some of those concerns. I have played other turn-based games from Sid Meier before (Starship) but not CIV. 

Overall I think CIV VII has a lot of interesting graphics and game dynamics to recommend it, but there are too many choice types / variables which affect how your empire progresses, that are buried in the UI / not easily discoverable as you start making your turns. And having tutorial reminders constantly popping up isn't a good solution either, because they become distracting after a while. One example of an opaque game dynamic is, even if you try to focus on developing science and core technologies (e.g. to help your military advance quickly), it's not clear how the AI empires, presumably forced to make the same kinds of trade-offs you are, can end up so far ahead (in a given category) in the same number of turns. it's almost like, even though it takes the human player 15-30 turns to develop a core tech or commerce ability, AI players somehow are able to develop those in fewer turns... and then, magnified over 200+ turns, ends up creating lopsided rankings across categories.

IMHO, the game would benefit from the option to turn off various kinds of cultural, environmental, and other impacts, so users can focus on the more intuitive dynamics of commerce, technology, and politics. While I'm sure if I played for 200+ hours, some of the obscure things would become more easily anticipated (via trial and error)... a player shouldn't need to play that long before gaining a decent overall understanding IMO. Don't get me wrong; there's many positive elements to the game, but taken as a whole series of dynamics, something doesn't feel right balance-wise.

The new Test of Time update honestly feels like something that should have existed from Day 1, but it has completely transformed the experience with the added customisation, improved pacing, and the excellent option to either evolve into a new civilisation each age or remain with your current one. The art style is fantastic, the UI and UX are now vastly superior, and the entire game now feels far more polished and cohesive. I was never a huge fan of Civilization 5 and 6. I actually found both of those games quite difficult to get into as a newcomer at times, whereas Civ 7 has genuinely made me appreciate and enjoy the franchise in a way I never really did before. It took a while to get here, but in its current state this is an incredibly addictive and deeply rewarding strategy game.

I like this game.

They swung for the fences with era transitions, and I'm glad they did. I am also glad they're reworking the system - it needed some changes. 

I like era transitions because it feels relatively "realistic". Eras in real history are bookended by disasters and happenings that transcend borders, plagues and crises of faith and warring nations that all throw the civilizations of the world into tumult. As the next era begins, the world has changed, including yourself. I love that vision.

It did not get implemented as well as it could have. My biggest complaint is that the crisis begins at "70% through the era" rather than being an issue that is dealt with through the entirety of the era, worsening as it progresses. I also don't like that the crisis is random, not fitting the theme of the civ/leader/playstyle you've chosen.

Military reset is good. I wish it was stricter. Cities/towns are an excellent system that makes it difficult for me to go back to civ 6 - allowing you to sprawl while not scaling micromanagement makes it so much fun to have a wide empire while still feeling tall.

UI leaves a lot to be desired. Figuring out the why something is the way it is is very difficult - seeing where resources are being generated, seeing the effect of placing specialists, new tiles. It's come a long way since launch, but there's a long way yet to go. Popovers are coming, which will help a lot. 

All in all, this will be an excellent game. They should have cooked longer, and thought harder about the era system, but they will bring it back - in a lot of ways, they already have. 05/19/26, this game is worth playing, especially if you can catch it on sale.

One thing I don't see much of is that the game is very well optimized.

citations.review_text:
After the latest update, I do like the game.

Fundamentally if I wanted to play an old CIV game, I would just open them up - they still exist. But I find myself liking a lot of the new features and thinking I can't play without them.

Commanders are great and combat is streamlined.
I actually like the ages - they break things up, change the gameplay completely and offer a reset. And they give you things to look forward to each age (Rather than waiting for your age and then executing like before). I do wish there were more combinations
Actually managing cities took a while to get my head around, but I like the cities to towns gameplay
There's always plenty to do in a game

I will say that I do think this game, like the last Civ game, is one major update away from truly being great. 

At the moment the issues I have is that the modern era doesn't really happen in a lot of games (it honestly seems like they built the game to have one more era and couldn't ship it in time)
Part of the above is that the victory conditions are a bit...meh. In my games, they all sort of just happen and that's it
A few systems (like independent powers) and religion need a bit more depth
An equivalent to loyalty needs to come back
And they need more Civ and leader combos as the current limited pack breaks immersion for a fair few leaders.

Also whilst I like the game now, I still want to say it was shipped in an inexcusable state as someone who bought it early on. Things like not being able to see the map to know what city is being offered in a peace deal is just crazy.

The leader and civ combinations allow me a level of flexibility and custom options I've not had in previous versions and the commanders are an incredible addition. I've finished far more games of Civ VII than any others as the tedium of the endgame is greatly reduced.

Rocky start but has improved with each and every patch. There's a lot of things I actually prefer in this game when compared to previous Civs - Graphics, Commanders, Naval and Air warfare, diplomacy, independent states. Short Review: After a year and a half of updates, the game has reached a state where I can recommend it, but only if price isn't a concern for you. In terms of bang for your buck, you are still better off with Civ V or VI.

Long Review: So Civ VII changes the formula in ways that I personally quite enjoy and make it difficult to go back to previous Civ games. For one, Army Commanders make warfare in Civ VII more fun than it's ever been. Army Commanders remove a lot of the tedious micro of moving your army across the map and give you an easy way to reposition your army in combat. It takes some getting use to, but once you do you'll legit wonder how you ever did warfare without them. I went from a mostly peaceful player in Civ VI to someone who almost never finishes a game of Civ VII without declaring at least one war. By far the most fun part of the game.

The next thing I really like is the town and city system. In previous Civ games, each time you make a settlement, it's a full fledged production queue. Able to make units, important buildings, wonders, and so on. You generally wanted as many as possible because more production queues means more yields, more flexibility, and more space. However by the time late game rolls around, assuming you've been expanding properly, you'll be left managing dozens of production queues, trying to make the most of each and every one of your settlements. Turns would take 10s of minutes spent mostly clicking through production queues that you frankly don't need to win but have to manage anyway. Late game fatigue was real. Civ VII fixes this by having any new settlements you make start as towns, which do not have a production queue, are limited in the buildings they can make, and convert any production they make into gold. This allows settlers to be much cheaper, and gives you a pretty wide variety of playstyles to work with. You can make a bunch of cities, or you can have some towns feed into a couple of big mega cities and super cha…

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the onboarding experience and glossary as lacking, offering no clear explanation of core game systems.

citations.review_text:
Recommended, but wish I knew more going in

Comments below after first win down: Economic Victory, Rome into Chola into America, playing Franklin. Overall really positive but with some real friction points.

Good stuff:
Fun as hell honestly. Leader diplomacy, GDP, civ-specific civics, town/city split, all of it gives you more to actually think about than older Civs. Combat and mobility feel solid too (though settlers should not require a promotion to board naval commanders IMO). Independent village interactions are a nice touch. Big plus for me: strategic resources are just bonuses, not hard requirements to build units, so you're not stuck if the RNG doesn't hand you the right resource early.

Rough stuff:
UI is bad. Combined with a glossary/onboarding that doesn't really explain its own systems, it's very much a "figure it out yourself" game right now. Resource management sums this up: cool concept, miserable interface. Settlement placement has the same issue, you can't settle directly on resources, and with the Urban/Rural tile system that makes settling near mountains or big Wonders way more annoying than it needs to be.

Random notes:
Happiness is simpler than past games, which I like, but not a fan of the flat settlement-count penalty as a concept even though it's manageable. Single-civ (Time-Tested) runs are a good addition; haven't tried Syncretism yet. Crises need more teeth, they feel like a speed bump right now, not a real threat.

Bottom line: genuinely fun and ambitious, just rough around the edges in ways that hit new players hardest. Look up a UI guide before you start and save yourself the headache.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game cannot be played offline despite advertised offline mode functionality.

citations.review_text: Game won't even start up offline even though they said there was "offline mode"... as per my civilization VI review... theres no point in buying if you can't even play what you bought...

I've been a long time fan of Civ since 4 when I was a kid. As you can tell by my hours I've been pretty chill with Civ 7 for a while now, but I can definitely admit it's had a lot of issues (putting it mildly.) I do think the rollout has been poor, certain choices have been needless and greedy (locking civs and leaders for account linking, data privacy issues, the usual pre-order garbage, etc.) For what it's worth, with the latest 1.4 patch, the game is definitely in a good state, and I'd recommend it to anyone who loves a Civ game. They've genuinely taken in all the feedback and made changes, though it has taken a while to get there. Some big features are still missing like hotseat, city trading, canals, but a lot of those have been confirmed to be in the works still. And to their credit, they haven't released a DLC pack since they've really dug in to fix the game fully.

For the game itself, they've resolved every major issue I had, including limiting Civs per Era and fixing the stale victory system for something much more varied and replayable. So far since the update I've been a specialist menace with Inca, bought a culture victory through purchasing wonders as Mughal, and won an economic victory simply by just bullying everyone as the Republic of Pirates. It's been a lot of fun.

TL;DR: If it's too little too late for you, that's fair. But for me, I'm having fun with it, and if you're still willing to give it a shot, now's probably the best time.

At least until the inevitable expansion comes out.

claims.claim: Reviewers complain about overpriced downloadable content packs and aggressive monetization practices.

citations.review_text: 862 hours played and thousands of hours across all Civilization games and this has got to be the buggiest and least balanced game ever released. Buy this game if you want to pay money to not have fun and waste your time. Also, enjoy paying $30 for a half-baked, unfinished DLC every few months that breaks the game even more. This game is an incredible example of a developer trying a new idea, changing their mind after release, and shamelessly money grabbing with overpriced under-made DLCs every few months while they try to work out the kinks of the mess they made. No regard for balance. Cannot recommend in the game's current state and I hope this review gets read by everyone considering making a purchase of this game.

We lost the plot of a civ game. It was recoverable after that terrible launch state, but it's been a month since I last played or so now, and I genuinely don't want to go back. I think they may have milked the last penny they could out of money. I will not be buying their obscenely priced dlcs. That was my breaking point. 

Before it felt like the civ devs were the civ community with us. We all can plainly see now that they are at the very least under the thumb of corporate greed, or at worst, the driving force of that greed.
